traps.excerpt: interview P06 is compromised due to leading questions and acquiescence bias
Non-target segments: Single university students who rarely cook (e.g., P07)
retired couples with entrenched daily cooking routines and no desire for digital planning tools (e.g., P09)
One participant stated they would pay 30 euros a month after a severe holiday spoilage incident
Onboarding attrition risk: Requiring users to log existing fridge and pantry items creates high initial drop-off
Conversely, one budget-conscious cook views planning as an enjoyable ritual: "Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly. I would never want an app to take that away from me."
Household grocery misalignment: Lack of coordination leads to duplicate purchases or missing ingredients for planned dinners
The claim from snippet S08 that 97% of households would pay for automated meal planning is an unsubstantiated blog claim

criteria.justification: The brief is remarkably complete, addressing all six questions with substantive detail across clearly labeled sections.
Claims are consistently tied to specific sources with clear inline citations. The brief also expertly distinguishes between observed household behavior and stated preferences.

The brief shows excellent calibration by matching its confidence to the evidence, calling out unsupported market statistics, and explicitly advocating for further testing rather than assuming validated demand.
The recommendations are clear and justified, and the proposed experiments include precise target audiences, timeframes, and concrete success metrics directly tied to the riskiest assumptions.
The brief is tight, exceptionally well structured with concise bullet points, and free of padding, making it very easy for a product team to read and act upon.
